# verdigris — complete documentation

# Verdigris

> Verdigris is a single-binary web server and reverse proxy written in Rust:
> static files, HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2 (+h2c), TLS (manual, self-signed, or
> ACME/Let's Encrypt), load balancing, response caching, and middleware —
> all configured in one TOML file (`verd.toml`).

## Authoritative sources — don't guess field names

- `verd schema` prints the complete JSON Schema of the config. When
  unsure about a field name, type, or default, consult it — it is
  generated from the same structs the binary parses.
- `verd validate -c FILE` checks a config and dry-runs the full
  runtime build (read-only). `--format json` emits a machine-readable
  report; `--strict` fails on warnings.
- `verd init` writes a starter `verd.toml` (`-o PATH`, `-o -` for
  stdout, `--force` to overwrite).
- `verd fmt -c FILE` normalizes a config file's formatting (`--all`
  covers included files; `--check` only reports).
- `verd config -c FILE` prints the merged, interpolated, effective
  config with secrets redacted — check what shorthands, includes, and
  `${VAR}`/`${file:}` expanded to.
- `docs/book/src/reference.md` is a generated table of every field.
- `llms-full.txt` (repo root) concatenates this file plus the full
  reference for one-shot ingestion.

## Mental model

Top-level keys: `server`, `timeouts`, `limits`, `log`, `admin`, `acme`,
`upstream`, `cache`, `include`, `site`.

- `[server]` holds `listen` (`"ip:port"` strings or `{ addr, tls }`
  tables), connection caps,
  `security` headers, `graceful_timeout`. **`[limits]` and `[timeouts]`
  are top-level siblings of `[server]`, not children.**
- `[[site]]` = a virtual host set: `hosts` (or `default = true`),
  `tls`, `root`/`proxy` catch-all shorthands, and `[[site.route]]` tables.
- A route = matcher (`exact`, `prefix`, `regex`, `match`) + **exactly
  one handler** (`static`, `proxy`, `redirect`, `respond`) + middleware
  (`ip_allow`, `ip_deny`, `auth`, `rate_limit`, `cors`,
  `response_headers`, `security`, `compress`, `cache`, `limits`,
  `timeouts`). More specific prefixes win.
- Upstreams may be named (`[upstream.NAME]` clusters with `servers`,
  `lb`, `max_connections`, `health`, `timeouts`, `tls`) or inline URL
  lists.

## Recipes (each validates against `verd validate`)

Minimal static site on :8080:

```toml
[server]
listen = [{ addr = "0.0.0.0:8080", tls = false }]

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]
tls = "off"                      # plaintext dev site (default is "auto" ACME)
root = "/var/www/site"           # shorthand: catch-all static route
```

Everything as separate route tables (equivalent, more control):

```toml
[upstream.app]
servers = ["http://127.0.0.1:9000"]

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/assets"
static = { root = "/var/www/assets", index = ["index.html"] }

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/api"
proxy = { upstream = "app" }

[[site.route]]
exact = "/health"
respond = { status = 200, body = "ok" }
```

Load-balanced proxy:

```toml
[upstream.app]
servers = ["http://10.0.0.11:9000", "http://10.0.0.12:9000"]
lb = "least_conn"                # round_robin | least_conn | ip_hash

[upstream.app.health.passive]
failures = 3
cooldown = "10s"
```

TLS — pick one per site:

```toml
# inside [[site]] — choose ONE:
tls = "auto"          # ACME/Let's Encrypt; needs [acme] email + port 80 or 443
# tls = "self_signed" # throwaway dev cert per host at boot
# tls = { cert = "/etc/verd/site.pem", key = "/etc/verd/site.key" }
# tls = "off"         # plaintext only
```

```toml
[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"
storage = "/var/lib/verd/acme"
# directory = "https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"  # test first
```

Route middleware:

```toml
[upstream.app]
servers = ["http://127.0.0.1:9000"]

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/api"
proxy = { upstream = "app" }
rate_limit = { rate = "100/s", burst = 50, key = "ip" }
auth = { bearer = { tokens = ["${API_TOKEN}"] } }
cors = { origins = ["https://app.example.com"], credentials = true }
```

Cache in front of a route:

```toml
[cache.main]
tier = "hybrid"                  # ram | disk | hybrid
policy = "lru"
ram_bytes = "256MiB"
disk_bytes = "4GiB"
disk_path = "/var/lib/verd/cache"

[upstream.app]
servers = ["http://127.0.0.1:9000"]

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/media"
proxy = { upstream = "app" }
cache = { store = "main", ttl = "5m", stale_if_error = "5m" }
```

## Gotchas — names that differ from nginx/Caddy conventions

- `lb`, not `load_balancing`; `policy`, not `eviction`; `disk_path`,
  not `path`/`root` inside `[cache.*]`.
- `basic.users` is a `name = "hash"` **map** (argon2 inline, or
  `htpasswd` file for bcrypt), not a list of objects.
- `bearer = { tokens = [...] }` — plural array.
- `api_key` requires `location` (`"header"` or `"query"`), `name`, `keys`.
- `compress` has `algorithms` (`br`, `zstd`, `gzip`) and a single `level`,
  not per-algorithm switches.
- `include` takes a file, a directory (expands `*.toml` inside the
  dir), or a glob like `conf.d/*.toml` — a glob matching nothing is
  silently ignored. A file included via two paths merges once; an
  include cycle is an error.
- `hosts` entries are hostnames (or `*.suffix` wildcards / `"*"` with
  `default = true`) — no scheme, port, or path; `*.x.com:443` and
  `https://x.com` are rejected.
- A bare `{ tls = true }` listen table binds `:443` (no `addr` needed);
  `{ addr = "…" }` alone is plaintext.
- `host_header = "upstream"` (the default) rewrites `Host` to the
  upstream authority; `"original"` passes the client's `Host` through.
- `site.proxy` is a catch-all site shorthand accepting a cluster name,
  one URL, or a URL list; per-route use `route.proxy = { upstream =
  "name" | "url" | [urls] }`.
- `rate` specs: `100/s`, `600/m`, `10000/h`, `50000/day`, or a custom
  window like `10/30s`.
  `key`: `ip` | `identity` | `route` | `header:<Name>`.
- Durations: `500ms`, `10s`, `5m`, `1h`, `1d`. Sizes: `B`, `KiB`,
  `MiB`, `GiB`. Both are strings (`"10s"`, `"256MiB"`).
- Cache entries are keyed by scheme + authority (incl. port) + raw
  request target: HTTP and HTTPS, `host` and `host:8443`, and
  differently-encoded paths never share an entry.
- `${ENV_VAR}` and `${file:/path}` interpolation works for secrets —
  relative `${file:}` paths anchor to the config file's directory.
  `verd validate` resolves them, so exports/files must exist then.

# Verdigris

**Documentation for verd 1.0.0.**

Verdigris is a self-hosting web server and reverse proxy in a single static
binary: nginx-class performance with Caddy-like zero-configuration TLS and
a readable TOML configuration.

## What it does

- HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (plus h2c) on the same listener, downstream and upstream
- Static files with ranges, ETag/Last-Modified validators, precompressed variants
- Reverse proxy with load balancing, retries, health checks, HTTP upgrades (WebSockets)
- TLS termination with manual certificates, self-signed, or fully automatic
  ACME (Let's Encrypt) issuance — http-01, tls-alpn-01 and dns-01
  (Cloudflare) challenges, incl. wildcards
- Authentication (basic, bearer, API key), IP ACLs, CORS, rate limiting,
  compression (br/zstd/gzip), and a full HTTP response cache (RAM/disk/hybrid)
- Prometheus metrics, structured access logs, and an admin API with
  atomic config reloads (SIGHUP, file watch, or `POST /reload`)

## Design rules

- One binary, one `verd.toml`, no external dependencies at runtime.
- Configuration is validated before it can serve; a bad reload never
  interrupts traffic.
- Response bodies stream end-to-end; nothing buffers a whole body unless
  a feature explicitly requires it.

## For LLMs / tooling

The repository root ships `llms.txt` (curated summary + recipes) and
`llms-full.txt` (the whole book in one file), following the llmstxt.org
convention. Point a model at either, or give it the authoritative
`verd schema` JSON output — every config example in this book is
validated against the real parser in CI.



---

# Installation

## Prebuilt binaries

Release tags publish static musl binaries for `x86_64` and `aarch64`
Linux. Download the archive for your platform, verify the checksum, and
place the binary on your `PATH`:

```sh
curl -LO https://github.com/frontyard/verdigris/releases/download/v1.0.0/verd-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz
sha256sum -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing
tar xzf verd-*.tar.gz
sudo install -m755 verd /usr/local/bin/
```

Release artifacts are signed with cosign (keyless). The SBOM
(`verd-sbom.json`) is attached to every release.

## Debian package

Releases also publish `.deb` packages (`amd64`/`arm64`) wrapping the
same musl binary. Installing one creates the `verd` system user, a
commented default config at `/etc/verd/verd.toml` (a conffile —
upgrades keep your edits), and enables the `verd.service` systemd
unit, which starts on port 80 answering 404/421 until you add a site:

```sh
curl -LO https://github.com/frontyard/verdigris/releases/download/v1.0.0/verd_1.0.0-1_amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./verd_1.0.0-1_amd64.deb
sudoedit /etc/verd/verd.toml && sudo systemctl reload verd
```

State lives in `/var/lib/verd` (ACME accounts, issued certs, disk
cache) and logs in `/var/log/verd`. `apt remove verd` keeps them and
your config; `apt purge verd` removes everything except the `verd`
user.

## RPM package

The same layout is published as `.rpm` (`x86_64`/`aarch64`) for
Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE, and friends:

```sh
curl -LO https://github.com/frontyard/verdigris/releases/download/v1.0.0/verd-1.0.0-1.x86_64.rpm
sudo dnf install ./verd-1.0.0-1.x86_64.rpm
sudoedit /etc/verd/verd.toml && sudo systemctl enable --now verd
```

Unlike the `.deb`, the unit follows the distro's preset policy — on
most RPM systems it stays disabled until you `systemctl enable --now`.
`rpm -e verd` removes the package but keeps state and your edited
config (saved as `.rpmsave`).

## Docker

```sh
docker run --read-only \
  -v $PWD/verd.toml:/etc/verd/verd.toml:ro \
  -v verd-data:/var/lib/verd \
  -p 8080:8080 -p 127.0.0.1:2019:2019 \
  ghcr.io/frontyard/verdigris:latest
```

See [Docker & deployment](docs/book/src/docker.md).

## From source

Rust 1.88 or newer:

```sh
cargo install --path .
verd version
```

> **Crates.io note:** the package publishes as **`verd`** — `cargo
> install verd` installs the `verd` binary once the first crates release
> lands. Until then, installing from a checkout or a release artifact
> always works.



---

# Quickstart

Create `verd.toml`:

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:8080"]

[[site]]
default = true
tls = "off"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
static = { root = "/var/www/site" }
```

Run it:

```sh
verd run                    # looks for ./verd.toml, then /etc/verd/
verd run -c ./verd.toml  # explicit path
verd validate               # check the config without serving
```

The admin listener comes up on `127.0.0.1:2019` — `/health`, `/ready`,
`/metrics` (Prometheus), `/version` are available immediately.

## Try the admin API

Loopback is the default and needs no extra config — every request must
just carry a loopback `Host` (curl does this automatically):

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/health        # → ok
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/ready         # → ready (503 until fully up)
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/version       # → {"version":"x.y.z","commit":...}
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/upstreams     # → {"clusters":[...]}
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/config        # live config, secrets shown as ***
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/metrics       # Prometheus exposition
```

Set a token to protect it — **mandatory** if you bind beyond loopback:

```toml
[admin]
listen = "127.0.0.1:2019"      # or "0.0.0.0:2019" to reach it remotely
token = "${ADMIN_TOKEN}"  # interpolated from the environment
```

```sh
export ADMIN_TOKEN=change-me

# no token → 401
curl http://127.0.0.1:2019/health

# with token → ok
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  http://127.0.0.1:2019/health

# mutating endpoints work the same way
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  http://127.0.0.1:2019/reload
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  http://127.0.0.1:2019/purge -d '{"all": true}'
```

In Docker, `127.0.0.1` inside the container is the *container's*
loopback — `-p 2019:2019` can't reach it. Either bind the admin to
`0.0.0.0` with a token (and prefer `-p 127.0.0.1:2019:2019` so it stays
host-local), or query it with a shared-namespace helper:

```sh
docker run --rm --network container:<verd-container> \
  curlimages/curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:2019/health
```

See the [admin reference](docs/book/src/admin.md) for the full endpoint list and
reload semantics.

Change the config and reload without dropping connections:

```sh
kill -HUP $(pidof verd)          # SIGHUP reload
verd run --watch                 # or auto-reload on file change
curl -X POST localhost:2019/reload  # or via the admin API
```



---

# Examples

Each example is a complete `verd.toml` — copy it, replace the domains
and paths, check it with `verd validate`, then `verd run`. The HTTPS
examples assume DNS already resolves to the machine and ports 80 and
443 are reachable; drop the `[acme]` section and use `tls = "off"` or
`"self_signed"` where that's not true.

## Static site with automatic HTTPS

The flagship "zero-config TLS" case: a certificate is issued at first
request and renewed automatically; HTTP requests 308 to HTTPS.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com", "www.example.com"]
tls = "auto"                    # ACME issues and renews the certificate
root = "/var/www/example.com"   # catch-all static route shorthand
```

Security headers (HSTS, X-Frame-Options, …) come from
`[server.security]` defaults — nothing to configure. See
[TLS, ACME & redirects](docs/book/src/tls.md) and [Static file serving](docs/book/src/static.md).

## Single-page application

`spa = true` serves `index.html` for paths that don't match a file, so
client-side routes like `/settings/billing` work on refresh. Hashed
bundles under `/assets/` get immutable far-future caching.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["app.example.com"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
static = { root = "/var/www/app/dist", spa = true,
           cache_control = { "/assets/*" = "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" } }
```

## Reverse proxy to one backend

`site.proxy` is the catch-all shorthand — every request forwards to the
app. `X-Forwarded-For`/`X-Forwarded-Proto` are set automatically.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["app.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:3000"   # also accepts a cluster name or URL list
```

## Frontend and API on one domain

Serving the API under `/api` on the site's own domain avoids CORS
entirely. More specific prefixes win, so `/api` routes never touch the
static handler; `strip_prefix` removes `/api` before forwarding
(`/api/users` → `http://127.0.0.1:3000/users`).

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/api"
proxy = { upstream = "http://127.0.0.1:3000",
          rewrite = { strip_prefix = "/api" } }

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
static = { root = "/var/www/site", spa = true }
```

## Load balancing across replicas

A named `[upstream.*]` cluster gives you balancing, health checking,
retries, and pool tuning. `h2c://` URLs speak cleartext HTTP/2 (gRPC)
to the backend.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[upstream.api]
servers = ["http://10.0.0.11:8080", "http://10.0.0.12:8080",
           "http://10.0.0.13:8080"]
lb = "least_conn"                 # round_robin | least_conn | ip_hash
max_connections = 256             # per-member connection cap

[upstream.api.health.active]      # periodic probes on each member
path = "/healthz"
interval = "5s"
timeout = "2s"

[upstream.api.health.passive]     # kick members out on real failures
failures = 3
cooldown = "30s"

[upstream.api.timeouts]
connect = "3s"
response_header = "10s"

[[site]]
hosts = ["api.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
proxy = "api"                     # the cluster name
```

`upstream.api.unavailable` customizes the response (status, body) when
every member is down — handy for a branded maintenance page. See
[Reverse proxy & load balancing](docs/book/src/proxy.md).

## Multiple sites on one instance

Sites are matched by `Host`; a `default` site catches everything else
(including requests to unknown names).

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com", "www.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
root = "/var/www/example"

[[site]]
hosts = ["blog.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:9000"

# requests whose Host matches no site above land here
[[site]]
default = true
tls = "off"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
respond = { status = 404, body = "unknown host" }
```

## Redirects: www → apex and domain moves

`redirect_host` covers the plaintext leg (`http://www` goes straight to
`https://example.com`); the redirect route handles HTTPS requests to
`www`. `{path}` and `{query}` substitute from the request, so links
keep working.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]                          # canonical site
hosts = ["example.com"]
tls = "auto"
root = "/var/www/example"

[[site]]                          # www → apex
hosts = ["www.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
redirect_host = "example.com"     # http://www… → https://example.com…
redirect = { to = "https://example.com{path}{query}", status = 308 }
```

A permanent domain move is the same shape — every path 301s to the new
domain:

```toml
[[site]]
hosts = ["old.example.com", "www.old.example.com"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
redirect = { to = "https://new.example.com{path}{query}", status = 301 }
```

## WebSockets and other long-lived connections

Upgrade requests (WebSocket) are detected and tunneled automatically —
the only config that matters is timeouts: `request_deadline` would kill
a healthy stream and `send` bounds tunnel inactivity, so both are
disabled and liveness is left to the app's own ping/pong.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["live.example.com"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/ws"
proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:4000"
timeouts = { request_deadline = "0s", send = "0s" }
```

For SSE the same applies: streams must outlive the default deadline.

## Protected routes: auth plus an IP allowlist

Middleware composes per route — the LAN allowlist runs first, then
basic auth.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[[site]]
hosts = ["grafana.internal.example"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
proxy = "http://10.0.0.5:3000"
ip_allow = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.0.0/16"]
auth = { basic = { realm = "ops",
                   users = { oncall = "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$c2FsdHNhbHQ$3nGf8u5Z2p2mJx0yq9Rk3g" } } }
```

Password values must be argon2/bcrypt hashes — generate with `argon2`
or `htpasswd -B`; an `htpasswd` file path works instead of inline
`users`. For machine clients use `bearer` or `api_key` with `${VAR}`
interpolation. See [Middleware](docs/book/src/middleware.md).

When several routes share the same guard, move the middleware onto the
site instead of repeating it per route — routes inherit it and can opt
out with `enabled = false`:

```toml
[[site]]
hosts = ["grafana.internal.example"]
ip_allow = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.0.0/16"]   # applies to every route
auth = { basic = { realm = "ops",
                   users = { oncall = "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$c2FsdHNhbHQ$3nGf8u5Z2p2mJx0yq9Rk3g" } } }

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
proxy = "http://10.0.0.5:3000"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/healthz"
respond = { status = 200, body = "ok" }
auth = { enabled = false }                    # no auth on this route
```

## Public API: rate limiting and CORS

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[upstream.api]
servers = ["http://10.0.0.11:8080", "http://10.0.0.12:8080"]

[[site]]
hosts = ["api.example.com"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/v1"
proxy = "api"
rate_limit = { key = "ip", rate = "100/m", burst = 25 }
cors = { origins = ["https://app.example.com"],
         methods = ["GET", "POST", "OPTIONS"],
         headers = ["content-type", "authorization"],
         max_age = "1h" }
# auth = { api_key = { location = "header", name = "x-api-key",
#                      keys = ["${KEY1}"] } }
```

Preflight `OPTIONS` requests short-circuit before auth. `key` selects
what a bucket applies to: `ip`, `identity` (authenticated user),
`route`, or `header:<Name>`.

## Response caching

Cache stores are named and shared; routes opt in. Freshness honors
upstream `Cache-Control`/`Expires` by default, `stale_*` covers the
gaps, and authenticated requests bypass automatically.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"

[cache.main]
tier = "hybrid"                   # hot objects in RAM, rest on disk
ram_bytes = "256MiB"
disk_bytes = "10GiB"
disk_path = "/var/lib/verd/cache"

[upstream.app]
servers = ["http://127.0.0.1:8080"]

[[site]]
hosts = ["cdn.example.com"]
tls = "auto"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
proxy = "app"
cache = { store = "main", stale_while_revalidate = "30s",
          stale_if_error = "1h" }
```

See [Caching](docs/book/src/caching.md) for tiers, purging, and `X-Cache`.

## Fixed responses: health checks and maintenance mode

`respond` needs no backend at all — a cheap health endpoint for the
load balancer, or a maintenance page during a deploy. `exact` matches
win over prefix routes regardless of declaration order.

```toml
[server]
listen = ["127.0.0.1:8080"]

[[site]]
default = true
tls = "off"

[[site.route]]
exact = "/healthz"
respond = { status = 200, body = "ok" }

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
respond = { status = 503, body = "back in a few minutes",
            headers = { "retry-after" = "300" } }
```

## Local development

Plain HTTP, pretty logs, files from the working directory:

```toml
[server]
listen = ["127.0.0.1:8080"]

[log]
format = "pretty"
level = "debug"

[[site]]
default = true
tls = "off"
root = "./public"
```

To test HTTPS locally swap the listener for
`{ addr = "127.0.0.1:8443", tls = true }` and set `tls = "self_signed"`
on the site — a throwaway certificate is generated at boot.

## Splitting a large config

One file per site keeps `verd.toml` small. `conf.d/*.toml` is a glob —
fragments load in sorted order, tables merge recursively, `[[site]]`
lists append, and a scalar set twice to different values is an error.

```toml
# /etc/verd/verd.toml
include = ["conf.d/*.toml"]

[server]
listen = ["0.0.0.0:80", { addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"
```

```toml
# /etc/verd/conf.d/blog.toml — one fragment per site
[[site]]
hosts = ["blog.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
root = "/var/www/blog"
```

An empty `conf.d/` is fine — a glob matching nothing is ignored, while
a named file that doesn't exist is an error. `verd config` prints the
merged result with secrets redacted when you want to check what the
fragments added up to.



---

# Configuration

Verdigris reads a single TOML file. `verd validate` checks it and
dry-runs the full runtime build (read-only — nothing is created), so a
green result means `verd run` would actually start; `verd config`
prints the merged, interpolated effective configuration (secrets
redacted); `verd fmt` normalizes whitespace in place preserving
comments; `verd schema` prints the generated JSON Schema.

## Field forms

Every field accepts exactly one shape — a scalar (`workers = 4`), a
string list (`hosts = ["a", "b"]`), a table (`proxy = { upstream =
"x" }`), or a list of tables (`[[site.route]]`). On top of that, two
ergonomic conveniences apply broadly:

- **Scalar sugar** — most list fields also accept a single bare value:
  `ip_allow = "10.0.0.0/8"` means `["10.0.0.0/8"]`. `include` is the
  deliberate exception (always a list).
- **Shorthands** — fields with one dominant setting accept a short
  form that expands to the table with defaults:

  ```toml
  [server]
  listen = [":8080"]                        # all interfaces

  [cache.mem]

  [[site]]
  hosts = ["example.com"]

  [[site.route]]
  prefix = "/old"
  redirect = "https://new.example{path}"   # { to = "…", status = 308 }

  [[site.route]]
  prefix = "/ping"
  respond = "pong"                          # { status = 200, body = "pong" }

  [[site.route]]
  prefix = "/api"
  proxy = "http://app:9000"                 # { upstream = "…" }
  rate_limit = "100/s"                      # { rate = "100/s", key = "ip" }
  # rate_limit = { rate = "100/s" }         # same — `key` defaults to "ip"
  compress = true                           # default compression on

  [[site.route]]
  prefix = "/files"
  static = "/srv/www"                       # { root = "/srv/www" }
  cache = "mem"                             # { store = "mem" }

  [[site.route]]
  prefix = "/gone"
  respond = 410                             # { status = 410, body = "" }
  ```

  More one-liners in the same spirit: `match = "GET"` (a methods
  list — `match = ["GET","HEAD"]` also works, as does
  `compress = "br"`/`["br","zstd"]` for the algorithm set),
  `bearer = "${TOKEN}"` and `basic = "users.htpasswd"` under `auth`
  (the `tokens`/`htpasswd` fields), `retries = 3` (a
  `max_per_request` count), `unavailable = 503` (the no-healthy-member
  status), `health = "/hc"` on an upstream (an `active` probe),
  `log.access = "/var/log/x.log"` (just the output destination), and
  `host_header = { value = "…" }` (verbatim even when the value spells
  a keyword like `"upstream"`).

  Sites get the same catch-all treatment as `root`/`proxy`:
  `site.respond` and `site.redirect` materialize an implicit `/` route
  — a whole site becomes `redirect = "https://apex.example{path}"` for
  the www → apex case. At most one catch-all shorthand per site.
  `site.root` is the same idea for `route.static` — `root = "/srv/www"`
  is exactly a catch-all `static = { root = "/srv/www" }` route.

  `site.redirect` is the general catch-all redirect (template or
  table). `site.redirect_https` and `site.redirect_host` are narrower
  pipeline behavior, not routes: `redirect_https = true` upgrades
  plain-HTTP requests to https before routing, and `redirect_host`
  only changes the hostname *of that upgrade* — it is ignored when
  `redirect_https = false` or `tls = "off"`. Prefer `site.redirect`
  for anything else; the narrow names exist for the two one-line
  cases.

  The closed shorthand list and the cap — at most two shorthand forms
  beside the table — live in `docs/config-grammar.md`; the per-field
  types are in the [reference](docs/book/src/reference.md).

Network fields (`ip_allow`, `ip_deny`, `trusted_proxies`,
`rate_limit.exempt`) take CIDRs *or* bare IPs — `"10.0.0.1"` parses as
the host route `10.0.0.1/32`.

Disabled blocks: every inheritable middleware block understands
`enabled = false`, which opts a route out of a site-level (or global)
default — and all of them take the bare spelling too: `auth = false`,
`cors = false`, `rate_limit = false`, `response_headers = false`,
`security = false`, `cache = false`, `compress = false`,
`log.access = false`. `server_header = false` omits the `Server`
header (as does `""`; `"off"` parses for compatibility but is
deprecated and warns). A bare `false` carries no settings and never
warns; stray keys inside a disabled *table* do. `true` parses
everywhere `false` does — the table with defaults and `enabled = true`;
settings a block still needs (`auth`'s method, `cache`'s store) error
as usual.

`respond.headers` and `route.response_headers` both reach a `respond`
route but are different layers: `respond.headers` is the handler's own
verbatim response map (e.g. `location`, `content-type`), while
`response_headers` is the route middleware that edits whatever
response the handler produced — apply order is remove → set → add.

## Durations

Every duration field is a quoted string in humantime form — `"30s"`,
`"5m"`, `"2h"`, `"180d"` (`ms`, `us`, `ns`, `w`, `M`, `y` work too).
Bare integers are rejected: write the unit explicitly (`hsts_max_age =
"180d"`, not `180`).

## Match conditions

A route's `[route.match]` table adds conditions beyond the path:
`methods`, `headers`, and `query` maps — and when methods are all you
need, `match = "GET"` or `match = ["GET", "HEAD"]` is the shorthand
for `{ methods = […] }`. Values match exactly, or as a regular
expression when prefixed with `re:`:

```toml
[[site.route]]
prefix = "/api"
[site.route.match]
methods = ["GET", "HEAD"]
headers = { "x-internal" = "" , "x-env" = "re:^prod-" }
query = { "debug" = "1" }
```

An empty-string value means *presence-only* — `"x-internal" = ""`
matches any request that carries the header (to match a literally
empty value, use `re:^$`). Conditions only *filter* a route; they
never change which route wins on path specificity.

## Placeholders

`redirect.to`, `respond.body`, and `upstream.*.unavailable.body`
substitute request attributes written `{name}` (`redirect.host` and
`redirect.scheme` are literal):

| Placeholder | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `{path}` | request path (leading `/`) |
| `{host}` | request Host (normalized, port stripped) |
| `{query}` | raw query string including the leading `?` — empty when absent |
| `{method}` | request method |
| `{scheme}` | `http` or `https` |
| `{uri}` | path + query as sent (`/x?a=1`) |
| `{args}` | query string without `?` — empty when absent |
| `{remote_ip}` | client IP under the route's trust model (honours `trusted_proxies`) |
| `{request_id}` | the `X-Request-Id` — propagated or generated |

`upstream.*.unavailable.body` substitutes the same set. The set is
closed — any other `{…}` text passes through literally
(and `verd validate` warns, since it's usually a typo). Redirect
templates re-encode `{path}` before it lands in `Location`, so
`redirect = "https://new.example{path}"` is safe to copy-paste.

## Diagnostics

`verd validate` reports errors and warnings with the field path and
the file that set it (`site["name"].route[0]`, `upstream.api.servers[1]`).
Errors mean *will not work*; warnings mean *works, but probably not
what you meant* — dead config inside a disabled block, a catch-all
CIDR, a hostname-shaped redirect target. `--strict` promotes warnings
to failures for CI. `--format json` emits the same report as one
object; the shape is documented under [Command line](docs/book/src/cli.md).

## Includes

Split large configs across files:

```toml
include = ["conf.d", "extra-*.toml"]
```

`include` accepts files, directories (`*.toml` directly inside,
sorted), and glob patterns (`*` matches any characters in the file
name), and its entries interpolate like any other string —
`include = ["${VERD_EXTRA}"]` is valid. A named file or directory
that doesn't exist is an error; a
glob that matches nothing is silently ignored, so `conf.d/*.toml` can
be populated later. Tables merge recursively — `[[site]]` entries append,
`[upstream.*]` and `[cache.*]` tables merge by name — and **arrays
concatenate** rather than conflict. Scalars set to different values in
different fragments are an error. A file reachable through two include
paths (a "diamond") merges only once; an actual include cycle is an
error. Paths are always resolved relative to the file that writes the
`include` line.

## Paths

Filesystem paths in config are relative to **the directory of the file
that contains them** — never the process working directory. That holds
for `site.root`, `route.static.root`, `tls.cert`/`key`,
`auth.basic.htpasswd`, `cache.*.disk_path`, `acme.storage`,
`upstream.*.tls.ca`, and the log outputs, and each `include`d fragment
anchors to its own directory, so a config tree moves as a unit.
Absolute paths are untouched either way.

Two fields are exceptions by design: `static.error_pages` and
`static.try_files` name files *inside* `root`, so they stay
root-relative.

`${file:}` never belongs under a path-typed field or inside
`include` — it reads the file's *contents* into the value, so
`cert = "${file:/x}"` fails at load with a pointer to write the path
directly. `${VAR}` stays legal there.

> **Breaking change:** these fields used to resolve against the
> process working directory. If you relied on that, prefix the
> affected values with the config directory (or make them absolute).

## Secrets and environment interpolation

Secrets never live in the file itself:

```toml
[admin]
token = "${ADMIN_TOKEN}"        # from the environment
# token = "${file:/run/secrets/admin-token}"   # or a file
```

`${VAR}` errors when unset; `${VAR:-default}` supplies a default, as
does `${file:/path:-default}` when the file is unreadable. Relative
`${file:}` paths resolve against the directory of the file that
contains the reference — the same anchor `include` uses — so a config
tree can be moved as a unit. A literal `${` is written `$${`. `verd
validate` resolves them, so CI can catch missing secrets.

## Top-level layout

| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `include` | extra `*.toml` files/directories/globs merged into this file (paths relative to it) |
| `[server]` | listeners, connection caps, trusted proxies, security-header baseline, graceful shutdown |
| `[limits]` | global request limits (`header_bytes`, `body_bytes`) — sites/routes may override |
| `[timeouts]` | global timeouts — sites/routes may override |
| `[log]` | server log + access log (format/output/filter/sample) |
| `[admin]` | admin listener (`admin = false` or `enabled = false` to disable), bearer token, optional TLS |
| `[acme]` | ACME account + certificate storage |
| `[upstream.*]` | named upstream clusters for proxy routes — `upstream.name = "url"` or a URL list is the no-table shorthand |
| `[cache.*]` | named cache stores (RAM/disk/hybrid) for routes |
| `[[site]]` | virtual hosts: hostnames, TLS mode, routes, trusted proxies |

The full field-by-field listing is in the
[configuration reference](docs/book/src/reference.md).

## Editor integration

`verd schema` prints the JSON Schema for the config format. Point a
TOML language server (taplo, Even Better TOML) at it for completion,
hover docs, and inline diagnostics — save the schema next to the config
and reference it from the first line:

```sh
verd schema -o verd.schema.json
```

```toml
#:schema ./verd.schema.json
```

A schema generated from the installed binary always matches the
version in use.



---

# Static file serving

```toml
[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
static = { root = "/var/www/site", index = ["index.html"] }
```

- **Ranges**: `Range: bytes=…` single-range requests return `206` with
  correct `Content-Range`; unsatisfiable ranges get `416`.
- **Validators**: `ETag` and `Last-Modified` are emitted; `If-None-Match`
  and `If-Modified-Since` answer `304`.
- **Precompressed variants**: a `file.css.br`/`.zst`/`.gz` next to
  `file.css` is served directly when the client accepts that encoding —
  the content-encoded bytes are never re-compressed.
- **Traversal safety**: `..` escapes are clamped to the root; NUL and bad
  UTF-8 in paths are rejected with `400` before touching the filesystem.

Directory listings are off by default — requests to a directory redirect
to its `index` or return `404`.

`site.root` is a shorthand for exactly this — `root = "/var/www/site"`
at site level materializes a catch-all `static` route.

## Cache-Control and error pages

`cache_control` maps path globs to `Cache-Control` values. Matching is
by **specificity, not declaration order**: fewest `*` first, then
most literal characters — `"/app.css"` beats `"*.css"` beats `"*"`, so
a catch-all never shadows the specific entries:

```toml
[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]
[[site.route]]
prefix = "/"
static = { root = "/var/www/site",
           cache_control = { "*" = "no-cache", "*.css" = "public, max-age=86400" },
           error_pages = { "5xx" = "oops.html", 404 = "not-found.html" } }
```

`error_pages` maps statuses to pages inside `root` — exact codes
(`404`) or whole classes (`"4xx"`, `"5xx"`); an exact code wins over
its class.



---

# Reverse proxy & load balancing

```toml
[upstream.app]
servers = ["http://app1:9000", "http://app2:9000"]
lb = "least_conn"                  # round_robin | least_conn | ip_hash
max_connections = 256              # per-member connection cap

[upstream.app.health.passive]
failures = 3          # `passive = 3` works too
cooldown = "10s"

[upstream.app.health.active]
interval = "5s"
path = "/healthz"     # `health = "/healthz"` on the upstream is the same

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/api"
proxy = { upstream = "app", rewrite = { strip_prefix = "/api" } }
```

## Upstreams

- **Protocols**: `http://`, `https://`, `h2c://` (cleartext HTTP/2 with
  prior knowledge). ALPN on `https://` picks h2 automatically; a shared
  h2 connection multiplexes requests per member.
- **Balancing**: `round_robin` (smooth weighted), `least_conn`
  (`inflight / weight`), `ip_hash` (weight-proportional ring). Entries
  can carry `weight` and `backup`:

  ```toml
  [upstream.app]
  servers = [
    "http://app1:9000",                        # weight 1, primary
    { url = "http://app2:9000", weight = 3 },  # ~3/4 of requests
    { url = "http://app3:9000", backup = true },# standby only
  ]
  ```

  `backup` members serve only while no primary is healthy.

  When only `servers` matters, the table itself is optional:
  `upstream.app = "http://app1:9000"` is a one-member cluster, and a URL
  list or `{ url, weight, backup }` entry works the same —
  `upstream.app = ["http://a:9000", "http://b:9000"]`.
- **Health**: passive (kick members out after N consecutive failures for
  a cooldown) and/or active (periodic HTTP probes on `path`, honours h1/h2).
- **Retries**: `retries.max_per_request` replays idempotent requests on
  connect/connection-failure (`retries = 3` is the shorthand); a
  cluster-wide `budget_fraction` caps concurrent retries so retries
  can't amplify an outage. `unavailable = 503` sets the
  all-members-down status — the table form's `body` substitutes the
  request placeholders (`{uri}`, `{host}`, `{request_id}`, …), and
  statuses that forbid a body (1xx/204/304) are served bodyless.
- **Timeouts**: `connect`, `idle` (pool keep-alive), `response_header`,
  plus the route's `timeouts.request_deadline` and body read/write
  budgets.
- **DNS**: names resolve through the system resolver with TTL caching,
  failure grace, and re-resolution on connect errors.
- **Upgrades**: `Connection`/`Upgrade` tokens (e.g. WebSocket) are
  tunneled end-to-end; the tunnel closes when either side does.

Inline upstreams without a named cluster are fine for small configs:

```toml
[[site]]
hosts = ["app.example.com"]
proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:9000"        # catch-all route to an inline cluster
```

`site.proxy` also accepts a cluster name (`proxy = "app"`) or a URL
list. Inside a route, `proxy.upstream` accepts the same three shapes:
`"app"`, `"http://…"`, or `["http://…", …]`.

## Headers

Request headers can be set/cleared per route under
`proxy.request_headers` (bare `request_headers = false` disables it);
response headers under `route.response_headers`. Ops apply in order
remove → set → add.
`Host` is rewritten to the member authority by default
(`host_header = "upstream"`); set `host_header = "original"` to pass the
client's `Host` through, or any hostname (`host_header =
"api.internal"`) to force a value. `host_header = { value = "…" }`
sends a value verbatim even when it spells a keyword — the escape
hatch for an upstream literally named `upstream`. Setting `Host` via
`proxy.request_headers` overrides `host_header` (the validator warns).
Hop-by-hop headers are
stripped; `X-Forwarded-For` is appended when the peer is trusted
(otherwise replaced) and `X-Forwarded-Proto` reflects the inbound scheme.



---

# TLS, ACME & redirects

## Manual certificates

```toml
[server]
listen = [{ addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com"]
tls = { cert = "/etc/verd/example.pem", key = "/etc/verd/example.key" }
```

SNI picks the right certificate per host; a `default` certificate covers
clients without SNI. Cert files are watched and **hot-reloaded** — rotate
the file and new handshakes use it, no restart.

## Self-signed (dev)

```toml
tls = "self_signed"   # generates a throwaway cert per host at boot
```

## ACME — automatic certificates

```toml
[acme]
email = "ops@example.com"
directory = "https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"
storage = "/var/lib/verd/acme"

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com", "www.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
```

- Challenges: **http-01** (served on `/.well-known/acme-challenge/` over
  any plaintext listener), **tls-alpn-01** (answered during the TLS
  handshake on 443 — works when port 80 is blocked), and **dns-01**
  (TXT records published via a DNS provider API — required for
  wildcards, works with no ACME-reachable ports at all).
  `acme.challenge` picks the preference.
- Renewal runs automatically (lead time capped at a third of the
  certificate's lifetime) with retry backoff on failure.
- `[acme.on_demand]` (`enabled`, `allowed_hosts`, `rate`) issues certificates lazily
  on first handshake for allowlisted names, rate-limited to bound abuse.

### dns-01 (wildcard certificates, no public ports)

```toml
[acme]
challenge = "dns-01"

[acme.dns.cloudflare]
api_token = "${CF_API_TOKEN}"       # Zone.DNS:Edit + Zone.Zone:Read
# zone_id = "..."                   # optional — pins one zone
# resolver = "1.1.1.1"              # optional propagation-check NS
# propagation_timeout = "2m"

[[site]]
hosts = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
tls = "auto"
```

verd creates `_acme-challenge.<host>` TXT records via the provider API,
waits for them to appear in public DNS, then tells the CA to validate
and deletes the records afterwards. Zones are discovered automatically
by walking up each hostname's labels (`zone_id` pins one instead), so
sites spanning multiple Cloudflare zones just work. The token supports
`${VAR}`/`${file:}` interpolation like every other config string —
prefer it over a literal so the config file stays non-sensitive.

## HTTP→HTTPS and security headers

`site.redirect_https` (default on) answers plaintext requests with a
permanent redirect once a certificate exists for the host;
`site.redirect_host` overrides the target host. Security headers
(HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, …) are set globally under
`[server.security]` — `security = false` inside `[server]` turns the
baseline off — and refined per route under
`route.security` — HSTS is only emitted over TLS.



---

# Middleware

Per-route, in order: `ip acl → CORS preflight → auth → rate limit →
cache → handler → security/cors/ratelimit headers → compression`.

## Site defaults

Every middleware block also exists at site level and is inherited by
all of the site's routes — including the implicit `site.root` /
`site.proxy` catch-alls:

```toml
[[site]]
hosts = ["app.example.com"]
auth = { bearer = { tokens = ["${API_TOKEN}"] } }   # every route below
rate_limit = { rate = "100/s", key = "ip" }     # one shared bucket
ip_deny = ["203.0.113.0/24"]

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/public"
respond = { status = 200, body = "open" }
auth = { enabled = false }        # opt out of the site default

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/api"
proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:9000"
rate_limit = { rate = "10/s", key = "route" }   # replaces, doesn't merge
```

- A route block **replaces** the site block wholesale — except
  `response_headers` (`set`/`add` union, route keys win; `remove`
  concatenates) and `security`, which merge field-wise.
- `enabled = false` opts a route out of an inherited block; the bare
  spelling says the same thing for every middleware block —
  `auth = false`, `cors = false`, `rate_limit = false`, `cache = false`,
  `compress = false`, `response_headers = false`, `security = false`.
- A site-level `rate_limit` builds **one shared limiter** across all
  routes that inherit it — `key = "ip"` limits each client site-wide.
- IP ACLs **tighten only**: denies union, and a request must pass both
  non-empty allow lists — a route can't widen a site ACL.
- `timeouts`, `limits`, and `security` also layer global → site →
  route.

## IP ACLs

```toml
[[site.route]]
prefix = "/internal"
ip_allow = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.0.0/16"]
ip_deny = ["10.0.0.9/32"]
```

Client IP honours `X-Forwarded-For` only from `trusted_proxies`. A
site's `trusted_proxies` **replaces** the global
`server.trusted_proxies` list — set the full CIDR set on the site, not
just the additions.

## Response headers

`response_headers` (and `proxy.request_headers` upstream-bound) apply
in a fixed order — **remove → set → add** — so a same-named
`remove`+`set` means "clear the incoming value, write ours".

## Authentication

```toml
auth = { basic = { realm = "ops",
                   users = { ned = "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$c2FsdHNhbHQ$3nGf8u5Z2p2mJx0yq9Rk3g" } }}
# or: auth = { bearer = { tokens = ["${API_TOKEN}"] } }
# or the token shorthand: auth = { bearer = "${API_TOKEN}" }
# or: auth = { api_key = { location = "header", name = "x-api-key", keys = ["${KEY1}"] } }
```

Basic-auth passwords must be argon2id or bcrypt hashes (plaintext is
rejected at validation). `basic = "users.htpasswd"` is shorthand for
`{ htpasswd = "users.htpasswd" }` — a bcrypt `$2y$` file instead of
inline users. The authenticated identity rides request extensions into
handlers, the access log, and rate-limit keys.

## CORS

```toml
cors = { origins = ["https://app.example.com", "*.staging.example.com"],
         methods = ["GET","POST"], headers = ["content-type"],
         credentials = true, max_age = "1h" }
```

Preflights short-circuit before auth; actual responses get ACAO/ACAC and
a `Vary: Origin`.

## Rate limiting

```toml
rate_limit = { rate = "10/s", burst = 20, key = "identity" }
# or: rate_limit = { rate = "600/m", burst = 20, key = "header:x-api-key" }
```

Token bucket per key (`ip`, `identity`, or `header:<name>`), with
`dry_run` (log-but-allow), `exempt` CIDRs, and `RateLimit-*` headers.
Idle buckets are swept automatically.

## Compression

```toml
compress = { types = ["text/*", "application/json"], min_bytes = "1KiB",
             algorithms = ["br", "zstd", "gzip"], level = 5 }
# or just: compress = true
# or pick algorithms: compress = "br" / compress = ["br", "zstd"]
```

Streams br/zstd/gzip by `Accept-Encoding` q-values; skips small bodies,
precompressed content, ranges, HEAD, no-transform responses, and upgrades.



---

# Caching

A full HTTP response cache in front of any handler — static files and
proxied responses alike.

```toml
[cache.main]
tier = "hybrid"            # ram | disk | hybrid
policy = "lru"           # lru | lfu | fifo
ram_bytes = "256MiB"
disk_bytes = "4GiB"
disk_path = "/var/lib/verd/cache"
max_object_bytes = "16MiB"

[[site.route]]
prefix = "/assets"
proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:8080"   # cache sits in front of any handler
cache = { store = "main", ttl = "5m",
          stale_while_revalidate = "30s", stale_if_error = "5m" }
```

A bare `cache = "main"` enables the store with default settings.

## Semantics

Honours `Cache-Control`/`Expires` on responses, request directives
(`no-cache`, `no-store`, `only-if-cached`, `max-age`, `max-stale`,
`min-fresh`), `Vary` (plus forced `vary_headers`), client conditionals
(`If-None-Match`/`If-Modified-Since` → `304`), heuristic freshness,
negative caching (`negative_ttl`, 404s et al. via `cache_statuses`),
`must-revalidate`, `stale-while-revalidate` (background refresh) and
`stale-if-error`. HEAD shares GET's entry.

Requests for the same key **coalesce**: one leader fetches, followers
wait and read the committed entry.

## Bypass and purge

`cache.bypass` skips the cache by path glob, method, request header, or
for authenticated requests (default). `X-Cache: HIT|MISS|STALE|BYPASS`
is emitted by default — `x_cache = false` suppresses it.

```sh
curl -XPOST localhost:2019/purge -d '{"store":"main","prefix":"/assets"}'
curl -XPOST localhost:2019/purge -d '{"all":true}'
```

## Tiers

- `ram`: in-memory, budgeted by bytes/items.
- `disk`: content-addressed object files with self-describing heads; the
  index rebuilds at boot, dropping corrupt or partial files.
- `hybrid`: RAM read-through in front of disk; hits promote, the disk
  copy is authoritative.



---

# Observability

## Server log

Diagnostics from the server itself — startup, listener binds, reloads,
upstream health transitions — go through `[log]`:

```toml
[log]
level = "info"               # error / warn / info / debug / trace,
                             # or full tracing EnvFilter syntax:
                             # "verd=debug,hyper=warn,tower_http=off"
format = "json"              # or "pretty"
output = "stderr"            # or "stdout" / a file path
```

Precedence: `--log-level` / `VERD_LOG` (command line) overrides
`[log] level`, which overrides the built-in `info` default. Format and
output have no flag — they only come from the config file.

File output is appended and reopened on **SIGUSR1** (logrotate), same
as the access log.

## Access log

One JSON record per request (default), emitted when the response body
finishes — bytes and duration are what actually went over the wire. A
client that disconnects mid-body is logged as `499`.

```toml
[log.access]
format = "json"            # or "pretty"
output = "/var/log/verd/access.log"   # or "stdout" / "stderr"
filter = 'path != "/healthz" && status != 404'
sample = 0.25              # deterministic fraction
# access = "/var/log/verd/access.log" is the same thing when the rest
# is default — access = false disables logging entirely
```

Fields: `ts` (RFC 3339 UTC), `req_id`, `client_ip`, `method`, `host`,
`path`, `proto`, `tls`, `route`, `status`, `bytes`, `duration_ms`,
`user_agent`, `referer`, `upstream`, `cache`, `identity`.

Filter terms support `=`/`!=`/`==`, `=~`/`!~` globs, and `>`/`<`/`>=`/`<=`
on `path`, `host`, `method`, `status`, `upstream`, `cache`, `identity`.
Terms join with `&&` only — there is no `||` (for disjunctions, filter
downstream in the collector).

File output is reopened on **SIGUSR1** (logrotate).

## Metrics

`GET /metrics` on the admin listener exposes Prometheus text format.
Labels are deliberately bounded — route ids, store/cluster/member names
from the config, exact status codes, and a `method` label that folds
non-standard methods into `OTHER` — never hosts, paths or headers.
Metric handles are resolved once per config object, so steady-state
emission is a few atomic ops rather than a registry lookup per request.

- `verd_requests_total{method,status,route}` — completed requests
  (client aborts count as `status="499"`)
- `verd_request_duration_seconds{route}` — fixed-bucket histogram
  (`le` series for `histogram_quantile`), plus
  `verd_response_bytes_total` / `verd_request_bytes_total` per route
- `verd_cache_requests_total{store,result}`, `verd_cache_bytes`,
  `verd_cache_items`
- `verd_upstream_requests_total{cluster,member,result}`,
  `verd_upstream_healthy`, `verd_upstream_inflight`,
  `verd_upstream_duration_seconds`
- `verd_active_connections`, `verd_connections_total`,
  `verd_connections_rejected_total`, `verd_active_requests`,
  `verd_tls_handshake_errors_total`
- `verd_tunnels_total`, `verd_tunnels_active`,
  `verd_tunnel_bytes_total{direction}` — upgraded WebSocket/CONNECT
  tunnels
- `verd_ratelimit_rejected_total`, `verd_acme_issuance_total`,
  `verd_cert_expiry_seconds`, `verd_config_reloads_total{result}`
- `verd_process_resident_bytes`, `verd_process_cpu_seconds_total`,
  `verd_process_open_fds`, `verd_process_threads`,
  `verd_uptime_seconds` (read from `/proc` every 5 s)
- `verd_build_info{version,commit}` — always `1`

## Probes

`GET /health` is always `200 ok` (process alive). `GET /ready` returns
`503` until the config is built and every listener is bound — wire it to
your load balancer's readiness check.



---

# Admin API & lifecycle

The admin listener (`admin.listen`, default `127.0.0.1:2019`) is a
separate HTTP service from the data plane.

```toml
[admin]
listen = "127.0.0.1:2019"    # ":2019" binds all interfaces
# listen = ["127.0.0.1:2019", "127.0.0.1:2020"]   # or several —
                               # one admin API served on each address
token = "${ADMIN_TOKEN}"     # mandatory when listen is not loopback
tls = { cert = "admin.pem", key = "admin.key" }   # optional
# tls = "self_signed"        # or a generated localhost cert for dev
```

`admin = false` disables the listener entirely (the table's
`enabled = false` says the same thing); leftover `[admin]` fields are
reported as dead config.

| Endpoint | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | liveness |
| `GET /ready` | readiness (bind to your LB health check) |
| `GET /metrics` | Prometheus exposition |
| `GET /version` | version + commit |
| `GET /config` | the live config; secret values rendered `***` |
| `GET /upstreams` | per-cluster member health, drain, in-flight |
| `POST /reload` | re-read the config file, swap generations |
| `POST /purge` | `{store?, key? \| prefix? \| all:true}` cache purge |
| `POST /upstreams/{cluster}/{member}/drain` | remove member from rotation |
| `POST /upstreams/{cluster}/{member}/undrain` | restore member |

`{member}` is a member index or URL authority.

## Trust model

`token` is the only real authenticator. When it is set, every request
needs the bearer. When it is unset — allowed only because validation
*requires* `token` for any non-loopback `listen` — the gate is
header-based: `Host` must name a loopback interface (defeats DNS
rebinding through a browser), and mutating methods reject the
`Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` markers a cross-origin page cannot
suppress. These checks stop **browsers**; they stop nothing else.

**Any local process can manage a tokenless listener.** Loopback is
shared by every uid on the machine, and a non-browser client simply
sends `Host: localhost` itself — `/reload`, `/purge`,
`/upstreams/.../drain` and read access to `/config` are all open to
it. If the host runs other software or other users, set `token`, or
wall the port off from other uids (netfilter `owner` match, a
dedicated network namespace, socket activation). A unix-domain
socket form — where filesystem permissions make the listener
owner-uid-only by construction — is planned; the design is recorded
in `docs/ROADMAP.md`.

`/version` reports `{"version":"x.y.z","commit":<sha-or-null>}` —
`version` is the crate version baked at compile time, `commit` is the
git SHA when the build sets `VERD_GIT_SHA` (release binaries do;
locally `null` otherwise). `verd version` prints the same fields.

## Reload semantics

SIGHUP, `POST /reload`, or `--watch` file changes all take the same path:

1. Re-read and validate the config. Errors keep the old generation —
   traffic is never interrupted.
2. Build a new runtime, reusing unchanged cache stores (RAM contents and
   disk indexes survive reloads).
3. Swap the runtime atomically; sockets that still match the listener set
   keep accepting against the new config, removed sockets drain, added
   sockets bind. Any bind failure aborts the whole reload.
4. In-flight requests finish on the old generation; new connections get
   the new one immediately.

The admin listener itself (address + TLS pair) is boot-fixed; the bearer
token rotates with the config. The `[log]` sink is boot-fixed too —
level/format/output changes need a restart.



---

# Docker & deployment

The published image is a static musl binary on `distroless/static`,
running as `nonroot` with a read-only root filesystem.

## Writable directories

| Path | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `/var/lib/verd` | disk-cache objects, ACME account + certificates |
| `/var/log/verd` | access-log files (or log to stdout) |
| `/etc/verd` | config + manual cert files (mount **read-only**) |

```sh
docker run --read-only \
  -v $PWD/verd.toml:/etc/verd/verd.toml:ro \
  -v verd-data:/var/lib/verd \
  -p 80:8080 -p 127.0.0.1:2019:2019 \
  ghcr.io/frontyard/verdigris:latest
```

## Compose

`docker-compose.yml` at the repo root runs a demo: static site, an
`http-echo` upstream behind `/api`, and the admin API on
`127.0.0.1:2019`.

## systemd

`packaging/verd.service` — `ExecReload` uses SIGHUP for config reload
and SIGUSR1 for access-log reopen, `ProtectSystem=strict` with
`ReadWritePaths` limited to state/log/config dirs, and
`AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` for ports <1024.



---

# Tuning

## Limits

```toml
[limits]
header_bytes = "32KiB"        # total request header size
body_bytes = "10MiB"          # per-route override: route.limits.body_bytes

[server]
max_connections = 100000
max_connections_per_ip = 1000
```

## Timeouts

```toml
[timeouts]
header_read = "10s"    # until the first request's headers arrive
idle = "60s"           # keep-alive between requests
body_read = "30s"
send = "60s"           # write inactivity; also bounds silent tunnels
tls_handshake = "10s"
request_deadline = "0" # whole-request cap, per route; 0 = none
```

## Practical notes

- Bodies stream — `body_bytes` caps size without buffering.
- Keep-alive and h2 multiplexing are on by default; no tuning needed for
  typical workloads.
- For high-concurrency proxies raise `upstream.max_connections` (per
  member semaphore) and `nofile` (see the systemd unit).
- RAM cache tiers are fastest; `hybrid` trades a small hit latency for
  surviving restarts. Size `ram_bytes` to your hot set.
- Rate-limit buckets are per key; `key = "identity"` with auth avoids
  NAT'd-IP collateral.



---

# Migrating from nginx / Caddy

| nginx | verd.toml |
| --- | --- |
| `server { listen 443 ssl; }` | `server.listen = [{ addr = "0.0.0.0:443", tls = true }]` |
| `server_name example.com` | `hosts = ["example.com"]` on `[[site]]` |
| `location / { root … }` | `[[site.route]] prefix="/" static={root="…"}` |
| `location ~ …` | `regex = "…"` on the route |
| `try_files …` | `static.try_files` (paths serve from `root` — no prefix rebase) |
| `client_max_body_size` | `limits.body_bytes` (route or global `[limits]`) |
| `gzip on` | `compress = true` |
| `proxy_pass http://app` | `proxy = "http://app"` or `{ upstream = "app" }` |
| `proxy_set_header X-…` | `proxy.request_headers = { set = { … } }` |
| `upstream { least_conn; }` | `[upstream.app] lb="least_conn"` |
| `limit_req_zone` | `route.rate_limit` |
| `auth_basic` | `route.auth = { basic = { users = { name = "hash" } } }` |
| `include sites-enabled` | `include = ["conf.d"]` (merges every `*.toml`) |
| `add_header X-…` | `route.response_headers = { set = { … } }` |
| `access_log /var/log/x` | `log.access = "/var/log/x"` |
| `return 301 https://…` | `route.redirect = "https://…"` (whole site: `site.redirect`) |
| `return 404` | `respond = 404` |
| `error_page 404 /nf.html` | `static.error_pages = { 404 = "nf.html", "5xx" = "oops.html" }` |
| `ssl_certificate(…)` | `site.tls = { cert="…", key="…" }` |

| Caddy | verd.toml |
| --- | --- |
| `example.com { file_server }` | `hosts=["example.com"] tls="auto"` + static route |
| `reverse_proxy app:9000` | `proxy = "http://app:9000"` |
| automatic HTTPS | `tls = "auto"` + `[acme]` account block |
| `basic_auth` | `route.auth = { basic = { users = { name="hash" } } }` |
| `file_server browse` | `static = { root = "…", listing = true }` |
| `encode zstd gzip` | `compress = true` |
| `respond 404` | `respond = 404` |
| `redir https://apex{uri}` | `site.redirect = "https://apex{path}{query}"` |

Wildcard hosts (`*.example.com`), regex routes, per-site trusted proxies,
and multi-site host routing match nginx semantics — the config reference
covers each knob.



---

# Upgrading

- **Binary**: replace the binary (or image tag) and send `SIGTERM`; the
  drain window lets in-flight requests finish. Rolling upgrades across a
  cluster need no special handling — `/ready` drops first.
- **Config**: `verd validate` after upgrading catches renamed or
  removed fields before rollout. The schema is versioned with the binary;
  `verd schema` prints it.
- **State**: disk caches and ACME storage are forward-compatible within
  V1; entries that fail to parse are dropped at rebuild, never fatal.
- Zero-downtime config changes never need a binary restart — see
  [reload semantics](docs/book/src/admin.md#reload-semantics).
- **What changed**: each release is documented in the repository's
  `CHANGELOG.md` (Keep a Changelog format); the GitHub release notes are
  generated from it automatically.



---

# Operations

## Day-to-day

- **Reload config**: `systemctl reload verd` (SIGHUP), `POST /reload`,
  or `--watch`. All are atomic; a bad file keeps the old generation.
  `${VAR}`/`${file:…}` interpolation runs at load — env-var changes are
  not file events, so `--watch` alone doesn't catch them; send SIGHUP
  or `POST /reload` after editing an env var.
- **Rotate access logs**: move the file, then `kill -USR1` (the systemd
  unit wires this as the second `ExecReload`).
- **Rotate TLS certs**: overwrite the PEM files — the watcher hot-loads
  them for new handshakes.
- **Drain a backend**: `POST /upstreams/<cluster>/<member>/drain` before
  maintenance; `/undrain` to restore.

## Debugging

- `VERD_LOG=debug` (or `--log-level`) for structured tracing on stderr.
- `GET /config` (admin) shows the *effective* merged config with secrets
  redacted — check this before assuming a key applied.
- `GET /upstreams` shows member health/drain/in-flight live.
- Access-log `499` = the client hung up mid-body, not a server error.
- Metrics `verd_upstream_healthy{member=…} = 0` marks members out of
  rotation (active probe failing, passive cooldown, or drained).

## Failure modes

- Reload bind failure → reload aborts, old generation keeps serving.
- Cache disk corruption → entries dropped at boot rebuild; serving
  continues with an empty cache.
- ACME failure → issuance retries with backoff; sites with no cert yet
  serve HTTP until one exists.



---

# Command line

`verd` is a single binary with seven subcommands.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `verd run` | Start the server. |
| `verd validate` | Check a config file for errors and dry-run the full runtime build (read-only); exits non-zero on failure. |
| `verd init` | Write a starter `verd.toml`. |
| `verd config` | Print the effective merged/interpolated config as TOML or JSON (secrets redacted). |
| `verd fmt` | Normalize whitespace in a config file in place, preserving comments. |
| `verd schema` | Print the JSON Schema for the config format to stdout. |
| `verd version` | Print version, build commit, and target triple. |

## Flags

| Flag | Env var | Applies to | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --config PATH` | `VERD_CONFIG` | `run`, `validate`, `config`, `fmt` | Config file path. Without it, `verd` searches `./verd.toml` and `/etc/verd/verd.toml`. A directory argument errors with a pointer to `-c <dir>/verd.toml` — directories load via `include`, not `-c`. `-c -` reads the config from stdin — `include` and `${file:…}` resolve against the current directory and sources report `<stdin>` (`verd fmt -c -` prints the formatted document to stdout; `--check`/`--diff` compare instead). |
| `--watch` | — | `run` | Reload config when it changes on disk (in addition to `POST /reload`). Observes the parent directories of every loaded source — the config file, `include`d files, `include` dirs/globs, and `${file:…}` secret files — so atomic renames, editor save-swaps, k8s `..data` swaps, and newly dropped-in `*.toml` include fragments all trigger a reload. Events on unrelated files in those directories (e.g. a log file written next to the config) are ignored. The watched set is re-derived after each reload. Environment variables are captured at load — a `${VAR}` change needs `SIGHUP` or `POST /reload`. With `-c -` the config comes from stdin — there is no file to watch, so `verd` warns that `--watch` has no effect. |
| `--format FMT` | — | `validate` | `text` (default) prints diagnostics on stderr; `json` prints a machine-readable report on stdout — always `{ valid, strict, diagnostics, sources }`, plus `"error"` on load/dry-build failures. |
| `--format FMT` | — | `config` | `toml` (default) prints canonical TOML; `json` prints the same redacted JSON the admin `/config` endpoint serves. |
| `--strict` | — | `validate` | Fail on warnings too, not just errors. |
| `--check` | — | `fmt` | Exit non-zero if unformatted instead of rewriting. |
| `--diff` | — | `fmt` | Print a line-level diff of pending changes (implies `--check`). |
| `--all` | — | `fmt` | Also format every file reachable through `include`. Sources are discovered with a syntax-only walk, so formatting still works when a file has schema errors (a warning says validation was skipped); malformed TOML and missing `include` targets still fail. |
| `-o, --output PATH` | — | `schema`, `init` | `schema`: write the schema to a file instead of stdout. `init`: where to write the config (default `./verd.toml`; `-` is stdout). |
| `--force` | — | `init` | Overwrite an existing file. |
| `--log-level LVL` | `VERD_LOG` | `run`, `validate` | Server log level filter (`error` / `warn` / `info` / `debug` / `trace`, or an env-filter spec like `verd=debug,hyper=info`). Overrides `[log] level`; default `info`. |

The server log's format and destination are configured in the file
(`[log] format` / `[log] output`), not on the command line — see
[Observability](docs/book/src/observability.md).

`verd --version` prints just the crate version; `verd version` also
prints the build commit (when built with `VERD_GIT_SHA`) and target.

## Exit codes

`0` success; `1` config/runtime failures (including missing config);
`2` CLI usage errors. `validate` prints one line per error or warning
to stderr (or a JSON report on stdout with `--format json`); `--strict`
turns warnings fatal.



---
